children.text: This page explains the tag system used in this project. The annotations identify important moments in the
segment featuring Charles Hickson and the Pascagoula UFO incident. Tags help viewers navigate the video by theme, structure, speaker, and audiovisual detail.

The project uses tags to show how the segment turns a witness account into a televised credibility test. Some tags describe the structure of the program, such as the opening, signed statement, panel questioning, voting, and reveal. Other tags identify references to the UFO event itself. A third group of tags focuses on performance: gaze, facial expression, posture, humor, hesitation, and the ways panelists judge who seems truthful.
The tag names are intentionally simple. They use only words and spaces so they can work cleanly in AVAnnotate.
Structure tags mark the major parts of the video.
Used for the beginning of the segment, including the host’s introduction and the entrance of the contestants.
Used when the host reads the written statement attributed to Charles Hickson. This tag is important because the statement is presented as Hickson’s account, but it is voiced by the host.
Used for the section where the panelists ask questions to the three contestants.
Used when panelists explain which contestant they believe is the real Charles Hickson.
Used when the real Charles Hickson is asked to stand up.
Used for the short follow up conversation with Hickson after his identity is revealed.
Used for the end of the segment, when the host thanks Hickson and the impostors.
Event tags identify parts of the video that describe the Pascagoula UFO incident.
Used for general descriptions of the reported UFO encounter.
Used when the statement or questions describe the UFO craft, including its light, shape, landing, or opening.
Used when the statement describes the beings, including their appearance, height, skin, ears, or claws.
Used when the segment refers to Hickson being lifted, taken into the craft, examined, or returned.
Used when the video refers to Hickson’s young friend, Calvin Parker, who was present during the reported event.
Used for references to the examination aboard the craft, including the “large menacing eye.”
Used for references to hypnosis, lie detector tests, scientific examination, or attempts to substantiate the account.
Interaction tags describe the questions, answers, and exchanges between the host, panelists, and contestants.
Used when a panelist asks for basic information, such as location, color, sequence, or physical details.
Used when a question challenges the plausibility, truth, or evidence of the account.
Used when a question is framed as a joke or comic comment.
Used when a speaker asks for more detail or asks a contestant to explain something more clearly.
Used when a contestant gives a brief or minimal answer.
Used when a contestant pauses, delays, self corrects, or sounds uncertain.
Used when a contestant presents the story as true, firm, or unshakable.
Credibility tags identify moments where truthfulness is performed, questioned, or judged.
Used when a contestant appears to perform believability through tone, seriousness, directness, or composure.
Used when one of the impostors answers as if he were Charles Hickson.
Used for moments when the program tests who appears to be the real witness.
Used for moments that separate believing something from proving that it is objectively true, especially the discussion of the polygraph test.
Used when the segment refers to police, experts, hypnosis, lie detector tests, science, or people “of authority.”
Used when a panelist describes a contestant as sincere or convinced.
Used when a panelist judges a contestant as looking changed, serious, or marked by the experience.
Media tags describe how the television format shapes the testimony.
Used when the rules, staging, voting, or reveal structure of
shape the meaning of the segment.
Used when music, applause, jokes, performance, or theatrical staging turn the testimony into entertainment.
Used when Hickson’s account is filtered through the host’s reading, the written statement, the show format, or the presence of impostors.
Used when a complex event is reduced into a short television statement or brief question and answer exchange.
Used when the panel or audience is invited to judge who appears credible.
Used when humor expresses doubt, skepticism, or playful disbelief toward the UFO claim.
Used when music, applause, or other studio sounds shape the tone of the segment.
People tags identify important participants in the segment.
Used for the host’s introduction, reading of the statement, and post reveal questions.
Used for the real Charles Hickson, especially after the reveal.
Used when referring to contestant number one before the reveal.
Used when referring to contestant number two before the reveal.
Used when referring to contestant number three before the reveal.
Used for Orson Bean’s questions and vote explanation.
Used for Peggy Cass’s questions and vote explanation.
Used for Nipsey Russell’s questions and vote explanation.
Used for Kitty Carlisle’s questions and vote explanation.
Gaze tags identify visible eye direction or eye movement. These tags are used only when the behavior can be seen in the video.
Used when a speaker looks directly toward the host, a panelist, another contestant, the audience, or the camera.
Used when a speaker looks away, down, or to the side.
Used for noticeable changes in eye direction.
Used for visible blinking when it is analytically relevant.
Face tags identify facial expression and small facial movements.
Used when a contestant or panelist smiles.
Used when a lack of smiling is important, especially because Peggy Cass refers to contestant number two as someone who “never smiled.”
Used when a person appears solemn, tense, controlled, or serious.
Used for visible lip movement, such as licking lips or pressing lips together.
Used for visible or audible laughter.
Body tags identify posture, movement, and gesture.
Used when a person’s seated position, stillness, leaning, or body orientation matters.
Used for nodding, turning, tilting, or other visible head movement.
Used when a person’s hands are visible and their placement or movement is relevant.
Used for expressive body movement, including hand gestures or body shifts.
Most annotations use more than one tag. For example, a short skeptical joke by a panelist might include
. A moment where the host reads Hickson’s signed statement might include

The tags are not meant to decide whether Hickson’s account is true or false. Instead, they help viewers observe how credibility is created, questioned, and performed in the video. They also help separate what is said from how it is staged: the spoken testimony, the television format, the contestants’ behavior, and the panelists’ judgments all work together to shape the audience’s understanding of the segment.
